implementation_notes: Swift puts the pattern's key move into the language: guard requires an else clause that exits the enclosing scope, so the requirement sits next to the condition and the normal path is never indented - the language book states that using guard for requirements improves readability compared with the same check written as an if. Formatting is first-party as well: swift-format implements the style, and its UseEarlyExits rule lints and rewrites 'if ... else { return }' into 'guard ... else { return }' explicitly in order to keep indentation levels low. The classic if-based form is still right when the false branch must continue in the same block instead of exiting.
pitfalls: The guard's else must exit the scope (return, break, continue, throw or a Never-returning call); a guard that only logs and falls through does not compile, so the logging has to live inside the else before the exit.
Optional bindings written with if let instead of guard keep the happy path indented even after the Swift 5.7 shorthand; the formatter will not convert them unless the early-exit rule is enabled.
swift-format and the older community SwiftFormat have different rule names and defaults; committing both configurations produces output that fights itself.
